x-m-h3-01.title: The definite integral is 0, but is the area 0 too?
x-m-h3-01.goal: Know that the value of a definite integral and the area of a figure can differ, find the line where the problem in a solution starts, and choose the method that fixes the error.
x-m-h3-01.material: A student found the area of the region enclosed by the curve y = x² − 4x + 3, the x-axis, and the two lines x = 0 and x = 3 as below. (In words instead of a picture: this curve meets the x-axis at x = 1 and x = 3; when x is between 0 and 1 it is above the x-axis, and when x is between 1 and 3 it is below the x-axis.)
x-m-h3-01.thinking.0: Tell apart whether each line follows from the previous line and whether the setup itself fits the goal
x-m-h3-01.thinking.1: Explain the cause of the error with the meaning of the sign of a definite integral
x-m-h3-01.thinking.2: Compare and evaluate methods that fix the error
x-m-h3-01.prereq.0: Experience calculating definite integrals of polynomial functions
x-m-h3-01.prereq.1: Experience learning the relationship between definite integrals and the area under a curve
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line where the first problem occurs in the student's solution. (Some lines have correct calculations.)
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.hint.0: Read each line and check ‘does it come directly from the previous line?’
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.hint.1: Even if a calculation is right, check whether that calculation is what you wanted to find. In the interval where the curve is below the x-axis, what is the sign of f(x)?
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.line.0: Let f(x) = x² − 4x + 3, and let S be the area between the curve and the x-axis on the interval [0, 3].
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.line.1: Set S = ∫₀³ f(x) dx. (the definite integral of f(x) from 0 to 3)
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.line.2: F(x) = x³/3 − 2x² + 3x is an antiderivative of f(x).
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.line.4: So S = 0. Even though there is clearly a region between the curve and the x-axis, the area came out 0.
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.explain: The calculations (lines 3 and 4) are right. The problem is the setup in line 2. A definite integral is a value that counts the part above the x-axis as + and the part below as −, so the 4/3 of [0,1] and the −4/3 of [1,3] cancel and make 0. Area does not look at the sign, so the conclusion in line 5 is also an error that comes from that setup.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose the appropriate method for finding the correct area.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about why the definite integral became 0 by splitting into the upper and lower parts.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.hint.1: Estimate whether each method gives an actual value near 8/3. (Without a picture: the upper part fits inside width 1 and height at most 3.)
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.o.a: Find the definite integral over the whole [0, 3], then take the absolute value of that value as the area
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.r.a: The sum became 0 because the upper and lower parts cancelled each other. Even if you take the absolute value after they have been cancelled, the areas of the two parts do not come back.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.o.b: Leave out the interval where the curve is below the x-axis, and integrate only the interval where it is above
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.r.b: The part below the x-axis is also a region enclosed by the curve and the x-axis. Only its sign is −, but the area of that part is positive.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.o.c: Split the interval at x = 1 where the sign changes, take the absolute value of each interval's definite integral, and add them
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.r.c: This method splits at the place where the sign changes and counts the upper and lower parts separately.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.o.d: Find the average of f(0) and f(3) at the two ends, then multiply by the interval length 3 to get the area
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.r.d: The curve is not a straight line, so the average of the end values cannot stand in for the whole curve.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.explain: Splitting at x = 1 gives ∫₀¹ f = 4/3 and ∫₁³ f = −4/3, and the area is 4/3 + |−4/3| = 8/3.
x-m-h3-01.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to a friend who used this solution, telling them how the ‘definite integral value’ and the ‘area’ became different in this problem and what the correct area is.
x-m-h3-01.s.s3.hint.0: Describe the upper part and the lower part each in words.
x-m-h3-01.s.s3.hint.1: At the end, write the correct area as a number.
x-m-h3-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your explanation, is the reason the definite integral became 0 connected to the upper and lower parts?
x-m-h3-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say, with numbers, how you found the correct area?
x-m-h3-01.s.s3.model.0: A definite integral counts the part below the x-axis as negative, so the upper 4/3 and the lower −4/3 cancel to make 0. The area is found by splitting the interval at x = 1 and adding the absolute values, which is 8/3.
x-m-h3-01.s.s3.model.1: ∫ is a value that counts the upper part as + and the lower part as −, so 0 came out. The area is 4/3 on [0,1] and the lower part 4/3 on [1,3], so together it is 8/3.

x-m-h3-02.title: Back in place, but moved a lot
x-m-h3-02.goal: Check, by making several cases that satisfy the conditions yourself, that even if the change in position is 0, the distance moved can be greater than 0.
x-m-h3-02.material: A point P on a number line starts from the origin at time t = 0. Its velocity at time t is v(t) = t − c (c is positive). That is, while t is less than c it moves in the negative direction (left), and while t is greater than c it moves in the positive direction (right). Point P moves from t = 0 to t = b, and b is greater than c.
x-m-h3-02.thinking.0: Tell apart the change in position and the distance moved
x-m-h3-02.thinking.1: Make different examples that satisfy the conditions within constraints
x-m-h3-02.thinking.2: Explain the reason using the examples you made
x-m-h3-02.prereq.0: Experience learning the relationship between the velocity and position of a point moving on a number line
x-m-h3-02.prereq.1: Experience learning what a definite integral means
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.prompt: If point P is back at the origin at time b, choose the correct statement about the distance P moved from 0 to b.
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.hint.0: Think of an everyday example where the starting point and the ending point are the same (for example, going to school and coming back).
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how the point moves when the sign of the velocity changes.
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.o.a: The distance moved is 0 too. Because it is at the same place as the starting point
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.r.a: Having the same position means the starting point and the ending point are the same, not that it did not move in between.
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.o.b: It means the sign of the velocity never changed. It went in only one direction
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.r.b: If it kept moving in only one direction, it could not return to the starting point. Think about how the sign of the velocity changed.
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.o.c: It may have moved. If it came back, the distance is greater than 0
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that even if the ending point equals the starting point, the movement in between must be considered separately.
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.o.d: The distance moved is always equal to the absolute value of the change in position, so it is 0
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.r.d: The change in position is a value in which the leftward and rightward movements cancel. Its absolute value does not tell you the distance.
x-m-h3-02.s.s1.explain: The change in position adds up movements with signs for direction, so the going-and-coming-back amounts cancel, and the distance moved adds up everything regardless of direction. So even if the change in position is 0, the distance can be greater than 0.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.prompt: For velocity v(t) = t − c, make 2 pairs (c, b), with different c, for which the change in position from 0 to b is 0 and the distance moved is at least 9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.hint.0: For the change in position to be 0, what relationship must the area above and the area below between the graph of v(t) and the t-axis have?
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.hint.1: Split before and after t = c and think about each area. The distance moved is the sum of the two areas.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.var.c: The time c when the velocity is 0
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.ok.c1: c is positive and b is greater than c.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.fail.c1: c is positive and b must be greater than c.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The change in position from 0 to b is 0.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The change in position from 0 to b (= b²/2 − c·b) is not 0.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The distance moved is at least 9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The distance moved (= c²/2 + (b−c)²/2) is less than 9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.explain: If the change in position is 0, then b = 2c, and the distance moved is then c². So if c ≥ 3, the distance is at least 9. For example, if c = 3, b = 6, it moves 4.5 to the left and 4.5 to the right, so the distance is 9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one example you made and explain, using numbers, why the distance moved is not 0 even though the change in position is 0.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write the amount moved to the left and the amount moved to the right, each as a number.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write what happens to the two amounts in the change in position.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation show that the ‘going-and-coming-back amount’ is cancelled in the change in position and added in the distance?
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is the value you calculated with the numbers c, b you chose right?
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.model.0: If c = 3, b = 6, then from 0 to 3 it goes 4.5 to the left, and from 3 to 6 it goes 4.5 to the right and comes back, so the change in position is 0, but the distance moved is 4.5 + 4.5 = 9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.model.1: If c = 4, b = 8, the first half is 8 in the negative direction and the second half is 8 in the positive direction, so they cancel and the change in position is 0, and the distance moved is 8 + 8 = 16.

x-m-h3-03.title: If the terms get close to 0, does the sum stop too?
x-m-h3-03.goal: As data accumulate, revise the guess ‘if the terms get close to 0, the sum converges too’, and choose the statement that explains why that guess can be wrong.
x-m-h3-03.material: The sequence aₙ = 1/n gets close to 0 as n gets larger. A student said, “Since the terms get close to 0, the sum we keep adding, 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + …, will also get close to some number.” Call the value added up to the nth term Sₙ (the partial sum). The data are revealed step by step.
x-m-h3-03.thinking.0: Make a guess from partial-sum data, and revise the guess with new data
x-m-h3-03.thinking.1: Evaluate the idea of grouping and comparing
x-m-h3-03.thinking.2: Tell apart necessary and sufficient for convergence
x-m-h3-03.prereq.0: Knowing what the limit of a sequence and the partial sums of a series are
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose the most reasonable judgment.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, compare where the newly revealed data disagree with your earlier guess.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.hint.1: Pay attention to how the ‘amount of increase’ changes.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.info: S₁ = 1, S₂ = 1.5, S₃ ≈ 1.83, S₄ ≈ 2.08, S₈ ≈ 2.72, S₁₆ ≈ 3.38. The newly added terms are getting smaller.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most reasonable judgment from the present data?
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.after: All the terms are positive, so Sₙ only keeps increasing. An increasing sequence either gets close to some number or grows endlessly, but from this data alone it is hard to tell which.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Since the terms get close to 0, Sₙ will soon stop at some value
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: The terms getting smaller and the sum stopping are different. Even small amounts can pile up if you add them endlessly.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Sₙ grows, but I need more data to know whether it will stop
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You said only as much as the data point to, and thought about what more is needed.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: S₁₆ is about 3.38, so I conclude the sum stops near 3.38
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You concluded that the value seen up to 16 terms is the end. Terms continue to be added endlessly after that.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Sₙ keeps increasing, so I am sure the sum grows endlessly
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Increasing does not mean growing endlessly. 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … also increases but gets close to 1.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Looking at how much the sum increases each time the number of terms is doubled: S₂ − S₁ = 0.5, S₄ − S₂ ≈ 0.58, S₈ − S₄ ≈ 0.63, S₁₆ − S₈ ≈ 0.66.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does this data change your judgment?
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.after: If it increases by at least 0.5 each time the number of terms doubles, a suspicion arises that it keeps piling up and can grow endlessly. But this is only up to 16 terms, so it is not a proof yet.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The amount of increase settles at around 0.66, so it will increase by only that much and soon stop
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If it increases by about 0.6 every time, that amount keeps piling up. What matters is whether the amount of increase gets close to 0.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: As my first judgment, the terms get close to 0, so the sum will stop
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You did not reflect the new data. The new clue is that the amount of increase does not get smaller.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The amount of increase does not drop below 0.5, so it seems unlikely that the sum will stop
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You revised the first guess with the new data. It would also be good not to forget that it is not yet a proof.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.info: I tried grouping and comparing. 1/3 + 1/4 > 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2, 1/5 + 1/6 + 1/7 + 1/8 > 4 × (1/8) = 1/2, 1/9 + … + 1/16 > 8 × (1/16) = 1/2, and you can keep making such groups endlessly.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.after: In 1 + 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) + (1/5 + … + 1/8) + …, each group adds more than 1/2 endlessly, so the partial sum grows endlessly. Even if the terms get close to 0, the sum may not converge.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Still can't tell. I would need to calculate for larger n to decide
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The problem remains that calculating never ends. Comparing groups lets you make a statement without calculating endlessly.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Each group is greater than 1/2 and they continue endlessly, so the sum grows endlessly
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You judged by the fact that at least 1/2 keeps piling up with every group, endlessly.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Each group is about 1/2, so the sum gets close to about 1/2 too
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: There is not just one group; they keep going. What happens if you keep adding at least 1/2 endlessly?
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The terms inside the groups get smaller, so it eventually gets close to some number
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even if the terms get smaller, the sum of a group does not get smaller than 1/2.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.reflect: If you first thought ‘the terms get close to 0, so the sum stops too’, what data made you change that thought? Is the terms getting close to 0 a necessary condition or a sufficient condition for the sum to stop?
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.prompt: Based on the results above, choose the correct statement about the relationship between the terms aₙ and the series Σaₙ.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.hint.0: Recall the relationship between the partial sum Sₙ and the term aₙ (aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁).
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.hint.1: Test whether the example 1/n seen above fits each statement.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.a: If Σaₙ converges, then aₙ gets close to 0
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.a: This is a judgment that looks at what limit a convergent series puts on the terms.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.b: If aₙ gets close to 0, then Σaₙ always converges
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.b: The example 1/n is a counterexample to this statement. The terms getting smaller alone does not guarantee that the sum stops.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.c: If Σaₙ diverges, then aₙ does not get close to 0
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.c: 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverges, but its terms get close to 0.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.d: Even if aₙ does not get close to 0, Σaₙ can converge
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.d: If the terms do not get close to 0, the increments of the partial sum keep remaining, so it cannot converge.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.explain: If Σaₙ converges, then the increment of the partial sum, aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁, gets close to 0. But the converse does not hold. 1/n is a counterexample.

x-m-h3-04.title: I only added positive numbers, but the sum is −1?
x-m-h3-04.goal: Understand the condition under which the sum of an infinite series can be assumed to be a single number, and make a geometric series that satisfies the condition yourself.
x-m-h3-04.material: A student found the sum of ‘1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + …’ as below. All the terms are positive, but the sum came out negative.
x-m-h3-04.thinking.0: Find that the starting point of the error is an assumption
x-m-h3-04.thinking.1: Apply the condition for the sum of an infinite geometric series to exist, within conditions
x-m-h3-04.thinking.2: Make different examples that satisfy the condition
x-m-h3-04.prereq.0: Experience learning limits of sequences and sums of infinite series
x-m-h3-04.prereq.1: Experience listing the terms of a geometric sequence
x-m-h3-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line where the problem first occurs in the student's solution.
x-m-h3-04.s.s1.hint.0: Split each line into ‘confirmed facts’ and ‘things just assumed’.
x-m-h3-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write the partial sums S₁, S₂, S₃, S₄ yourself and see how they change.
x-m-h3-04.s.s1.line.0: Suppose the infinitely added sum S = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + … is determined to be some real number.
x-m-h3-04.s.s1.line.2: The right side is S with the first term 1 removed, so 2S = S − 1.
x-m-h3-04.s.s1.line.4: I kept adding only positive numbers, but the sum became −1.
x-m-h3-04.s.s1.explain: The starting point is line 1, which assumed S is a real number. The partial sums of this series are 1, 3, 7, 15, …, growing endlessly, so there is no number that the sum is fixed at. If you assume a number exists that does not, and transform the expression, an absurd value like line 4 can come out.
x-m-h3-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 pairs (a, r), with different r, such that the sum of the infinite geometric series with first term a and common ratio r is 5. (Decimals are allowed, r ≠ 0)
x-m-h3-04.s.s2.hint.0: First recall what range the common ratio must be in for the sum to exist.
x-m-h3-04.s.s2.hint.1: Decide r first, then adjust a so that the sum is 5.
x-m-h3-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The absolute value of the common ratio is less than 1, so the sum exists.
x-m-h3-04.s.s2.fail.c1: If the common ratio r is 0 or its absolute value is at least 1, the sum is not determined as a number.
x-m-h3-04.s.s2.explain: For the sum to exist, |r| < 1 is needed, and if the sum is 5 then a = 5(1 − r). For example, if r = 0.4, then a = 3, and if r = −0.2, then a = 6. a = −5, r = 2 only fits the formula a = 5(1 − r), so the sum does not exist.

x-m-h3-05.title: Two games with the same expected value
x-m-h3-05.goal: Know that probability distributions can differ even when the expected values are the same, and design a new game that fits the conditions and explain the basis for choosing.
x-m-h3-05.material: There are two games at a festival booth. Game A: toss a coin; if it lands heads the prize is 100 won, and if tails 0 won. Game B: draw one ball from a box; if it is a winner (probability 1/10) the prize is 500 won, otherwise 0 won. Both games have no entry fee, and call the prize the random variable X.
x-m-h3-05.thinking.0: Evaluate whether the expected value alone is enough
x-m-h3-05.thinking.1: Design a game (probability and prize) that fits the conditions yourself
x-m-h3-05.thinking.2: Say the reason for your own choice with evidence
x-m-h3-05.prereq.0: Experience showing the probability mass function of a discrete random variable in a table
x-m-h3-05.prereq.1: Understanding what the mean of a random variable represents
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct explanation comparing the two games.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the expected value of each game directly as (prize × probability) and compare.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write down what prizes are possible in each.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.a: A has a greater expected value. Because the probability of winning is higher
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the probability and did not also consider the size of the prize.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.b: B has a greater expected value. Because the prize is 5 times bigger
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the prize and did not also consider the probability of winning.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.c: The expected values are the same, but how spread out the prizes are differs
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out that even if the expected values are the same, the shapes of the distributions can differ.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.d: The expected values are the same, so the results are the same whichever game you play
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.d: The expected value is only the ‘average over many plays’ and does not tell you a single result or how spread out they are.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.explain: E(A) = 100 × 1/2 = 50 and E(B) = 500 × 1/10 = 50, so they are the same. But A is 0 won or 100 won, and B is 0 won or 500 won, so B is far more spread out.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 new games, with different winning probabilities, with an expected value of 50 won and a prize of at least 400 won. (If you win, the prize is m won; otherwise 0 won)
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.hint.0: Using the condition that the expected value is 50, write the relationship between p and m as an equation.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.hint.1: Decide m first and adjust p.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The probability must be greater than 0 and less than 1.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The expected value (p × m) is not 50 won.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The prize is at least 400 won.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The prize is less than 400 won.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.explain: p × m = 50, so if m = 400 then p = 0.125, and if m = 1000 then p = 0.05; the bigger the prize, the smaller the winning probability.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare one game you made with Game A and write which one you would rather play and why. There is more than one right answer.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write at the start of the sentence that the expected values are the same.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write one standard of your own, like ‘I am the kind of person who ...’.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you first accept that the expected values are the same, and then state your standard on top of that?
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Is your choice connected to a standard like ‘whether you like or dislike taking risks’?
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.model.0: Both expected values are 50 won, so the average is the same. I want to receive something steadily and often, so I would play A, which has a higher winning probability. A game with a small probability has a large variance, so I might not receive anything even once.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.model.1: Even though the expected values are the same, I like taking a risk and aiming for a big prize, so I would choose the game with a 500 won prize. Even if the winning probability is low, a big prize can come out at once.

x-m-h3-06.title: What top percent is a score of 85?
x-m-h3-06.goal: Know that to say a position in a normal distribution you need the spread as well as the mean, and choose values that fit the conditions yourself.
x-m-h3-06.material: The math test scores at a school are said to follow a normal distribution. The mean is 70 points. Minji got 85 and wants to know what top percent she is in. You can use the standard normal distribution table. (Note: in the standard normal distribution, the probability that Z is at least 2 is about 0.0228.)
x-m-h3-06.thinking.0: Decide whether the information is enough
x-m-h3-06.thinking.2: Make several values that satisfy the conditions
x-m-h3-06.prereq.0: The shape of the normal distribution curve (centered on the mean, symmetric left and right)
x-m-h3-06.prereq.1: How to read the standard normal distribution table
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.prompt: With only the information known now (mean 70, Minji 85), can you decide what top percent she is in?
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.hint.0: Recall how the position of 85 differs in a distribution where the scores are bunched together and one where they are spread out, even if the mean is the same.
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.hint.1: Think by removing the values one at a time to see which value is absolutely necessary to decide the percentage.
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.o.a: Yes. She is 15 points above the mean, so she is in the top 15%
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.r.a: You read the score difference directly as a percent. Depending on how spread out the scores are, the same 15 points means different things.
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.o.b: No. You need to know how many students took the test
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.r.b: The percentage is decided by the shape of the distribution. The number of students is not needed for the percentage.
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.o.c: Yes. In a normal distribution, being 15 points above the mean means the top 16%
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.r.c: The top 16% is when it is 1 standard deviation above the mean. If you do not know the standard deviation, you cannot know whether 15 points is that much.
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.o.d: No. You need one more value that tells how spread out the scores are
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.r.d: You pointed out that you need to know the spread as well as the mean.
x-m-h3-06.s.s1.explain: How many standard deviations 85 is from the mean decides the position. For that you need the standard deviation.
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.prompt: Compare two students from different schools. The student from School Ga (mean 70, standard deviation 10) got 85, and the student from School Na (mean 60, standard deviation 5) got 75. Which student has the higher relative position within their own school?
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.hint.0: Divide how much higher than the mean each student is by the standard deviation of that student's school.
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.hint.1: When the score difference is the same, how does the side with the smaller standard deviation differ?
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.o.a: The student from School Ga. Because the score is higher, the position is higher too
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.r.a: You compared the scores themselves. The mean and the spread differ from school to school.
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.o.b: The student from School Na. In terms of how many standard deviations, it is higher
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.r.b: You compared by how far from the mean in units of the standard deviation.
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.o.c: The two students are the same. Because both are 15 points above the mean
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.r.c: Even if the score difference is the same, if the standard deviation is different the meaning of that difference is different.
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.o.d: Can't tell. Because we do not know the number of test takers at the two schools
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.r.d: The number of test takers is not needed to compare positions.
x-m-h3-06.s.s2.explain: The student from School Ga is 1.5 standard deviations above the mean, and the student from School Na is 3 times. So the position within the school is higher for the student from School Na.
x-m-h3-06.s.s3.prompt: Set the standard deviation σ of the scores at Minji's school to an integer so that 85 falls within about the top 2.3% (at least 2σ above the mean), and make 3 different values of σ.
x-m-h3-06.s.s3.hint.0: Using σ, write as an expression how many times σ higher than the mean 70 the score 85 is.
x-m-h3-06.s.s3.hint.1: Also put in the integer right next to the boundary σ and check.
x-m-h3-06.s.s3.fail.c1: σ must be an integer greater than 0.
x-m-h3-06.s.s3.ok.c2: 85 is at least 2σ above the mean.
x-m-h3-06.s.s3.fail.c2: 85 is less than 2σ above the mean.
x-m-h3-06.s.s3.explain: For 15 points from the mean to be at least 2σ, σ ≤ 7.5 is needed. The integers σ are 1 to 7. The proportion with Z ≥ 2 is about 2.3%, so she is in the top 2.3%.

x-m-h3-07.title: What does a 95% confidence interval tell us?
x-m-h3-07.goal: Pick out the statement that interprets a confidence interval correctly, and find for yourself what sample size is needed to make the length of the interval fit a condition.
x-m-h3-07.material: The daily sleep time of high school students in a city is said to follow a normal distribution with population standard deviation 1 hour. When 100 students were chosen at random, the sample mean was 6.8 hours. The 95% confidence interval for the population mean is 6.8 ± 1.96 × (1/√100), so it is [6.604, 6.996]. (For a confidence level of 95%, use the coefficient 1.96.)
x-m-h3-07.thinking.0: Judge whether an interpretation is right or wrong with reasons
x-m-h3-07.thinking.1: Reason about the relationship between sample size and the length of the interval
x-m-h3-07.thinking.2: Check the boundary values yourself and make values that fit the condition
x-m-h3-07.prereq.0: Experience learning about the population, samples, and the distribution of the sample mean
x-m-h3-07.prereq.1: Experience seeing the shape of a confidence interval using standardization of the normal distribution
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct explanation of the meaning of this confidence interval.
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.hint.0: First point out what the interval is about (individual values or the population mean).
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what is being repeated when we say ‘95% probability’.
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.o.a: 95% of the students in this city sleep between 6.604 hours and 6.996 hours
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.r.a: The interval is about the population mean, not individual students. Individual students' sleep times are spread much wider than this interval.
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.o.b: The probability that the mean of a newly drawn sample falls in this interval is 95%
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.r.b: This interval is meant to capture the population mean, not to be the range of a new sample mean. The probability that a new sample mean falls in this interval is lower.
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.o.c: If you draw samples repeatedly and make intervals, about 95% of them contain the population mean
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out the meaning that it is the success rate when a method with the same confidence level is used many times.
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.o.d: Out of the 100 students in the sample, 95 sleep a time inside this interval
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.r.d: It is an interval for the population mean, not for the values of individuals in the sample.
x-m-h3-07.s.s1.explain: A confidence level of 95% refers to the confidence in the method: ‘if you draw samples repeatedly with the same method and make intervals, about 95% of them contain the population mean’. It is not a statement about individual students or a new sample mean.
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.prompt: With the same confidence level 95% and the same population standard deviation, what sample size should be used to cut the length of the interval to half of the present one?
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the length of the interval as an expression using n.
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare how many times the length becomes when n is changed to 2 times and 4 times.
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.r.a: You used the fact that the length is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size.
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.r.b: You missed that the length of the interval is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size.
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.r.c: The direction is right that increasing the sample size makes the interval smaller, but you did not check the proportional relationship.
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.r.d: You took far more than needed. Check with the formula how the length changes.
x-m-h3-07.s.s2.explain: The length of the interval is 2 × 1.96 × σ/√n, so to halve the length, √n must double, and so n becomes 4 times (400 students).
x-m-h3-07.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different sample sizes n for which the length of the interval can be at most 0.3 hours. (Confidence level 95%, population standard deviation 1 hour, n is an integer)
x-m-h3-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write the length of the interval in terms of n and write the condition for it to be at most 0.3 as an inequality.
x-m-h3-07.s.s3.hint.1: Also put in the integer values near the boundary directly and check.
x-m-h3-07.s.s3.fail.c1: n must be an integer greater than 0.
x-m-h3-07.s.s3.ok.c2: The length of the interval is at most 0.3 hours.
x-m-h3-07.s.s3.fail.c2: The length of the interval is longer than 0.3 hours.
x-m-h3-07.s.s3.explain: From length 2 × 1.96/√n ≤ 0.3 we get √n ≥ 13.07, so n ≥ 170.7, and since n is an integer, it is at least 171. If n = 170, the length is about 0.3007, which exceeds the condition.

x-m-h3-08.title: It says positive, but is the person really sick?
x-m-h3-08.goal: Pick out the information needed to find a conditional probability, and explain with numbers why the accuracy of a test is different from the ‘probability of being sick given a positive result’.
x-m-h3-08.material: A test for a certain disease came out ‘positive’. You want to know the probability that a person with a positive result really has the disease. Decide what information is needed to determine this probability.
x-m-h3-08.thinking.0: Tell apart needed and unneeded information
x-m-h3-08.thinking.1: Do not confuse the two conditional probabilities P(positive|sick) and P(sick|positive)
x-m-h3-08.prereq.0: Experience learning the multiplication rule of probability and the meaning of conditional probability
x-m-h3-08.prereq.1: Experience converting ratios into numbers of people
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the information that is absolutely necessary to find the probability that a person with a positive result really is sick.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.hint.0: Recall which two groups the people who tested positive can be split into.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.hint.1: Think about what ratios you need to know the size of each group.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.o.a: The proportion of people with the disease among all people
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.r.a: You pointed out how common the disease is among everyone. If the disease is not common, there may be few sick people even among those who tested positive.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.o.b: The probability that a sick person tests positive
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.r.b: You pointed out how well the test finds sick people.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.o.c: The probability that a person without the disease tests positive
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.r.c: You pointed out how often a healthy person wrongly becomes positive. If there are far more healthy people, this matters.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.o.d: The average age of the people who took the test
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.r.d: Age is not used in deciding this probability. Think about what the ratios that make up the probability are.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.o.e: The price of the testing equipment
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.r.e: Price has nothing to do with the accuracy of the test or the proportion of sick people.
x-m-h3-08.s.s1.explain: Those who tested positive are made up of ‘sick people who tested positive’ and ‘healthy people who tested positive’. So you need the proportion of sick people, the probability a sick person tests positive, and the probability a healthy person tests positive.
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.prompt: Suppose 1000 people took the test. 1% of everyone is sick, 90% of the sick people test positive, and 9% of the people who are not sick test positive. Roughly what proportion of those who tested positive are sick?
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.hint.0: Split the 1000 people into sick and healthy people and write how many are in each.
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.hint.1: Find the number of positive people in each group, add them, and compare how many of them are sick.
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.r.a: You took the 90% probability that a sick person is positive to be the same as the ‘probability of being sick given positive’. The condition is reversed.
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.r.b: You estimated by looking only at the ratio between the probability a sick person is positive and the probability a healthy person is positive. You missed that the numbers in the two groups are very different.
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.r.c: You thought that the information of being positive does not change the proportion. When the result is positive, it is higher than the first 1%.
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.r.d: You counted the sick and healthy people among those who tested positive and compared them.
x-m-h3-08.s.s2.explain: Of 1000 people, 10 are sick and 990 are healthy. For positives, 9 sick people (90% of 10) and about 89 healthy people (9% of 990), so among about 98 positives, about 9 are sick, which is about 9%.
x-m-h3-08.s.s3.prompt: Even though it is a test where 90% of sick people are positive, explain using concrete numbers like 1000 people why the probability that a person who tested positive is sick is much smaller than 90%.
x-m-h3-08.s.s3.hint.0: First write the numbers of people when you split the 1000 people into two groups.
x-m-h3-08.s.s3.hint.1: Write how many people in each group are positive, and compare.
x-m-h3-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In my explanation, can you see what two groups the people who became positive are made of?
x-m-h3-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare ‘sick people who are positive’ and ‘healthy people who are positive’ with numbers?
x-m-h3-08.s.s3.model.0: Of 1000 people, 10 are sick and 9 of them are positive. Among the 990 people without the disease, 9% of them, about 89, are positive. So among about 98 positives, about 9 are sick, which is much smaller than 90%.
x-m-h3-08.s.s3.model.1: Only 1% are sick, so healthy people overwhelmingly outnumber them. With 1000 people, there are 10 sick people and 990 healthy people. Even if only 9% of healthy people are positive, that is about 89 people, which is far more than the 9 sick positives.

x-m-h3-09.title: If a red side is showing, what about the back?
x-m-h3-09.goal: Revise your first guess (1/2) using data and analysis, and find which line of the guess is wrong to interpret conditional probability correctly.
x-m-h3-09.material: There are three cards in a box. One has red on both sides (the red-red card), one has red on one side and blue on the other (the red-blue card), and one has blue on both sides (the blue-blue card). You draw one card at random and put one side on the desk, and red is showing. Think about the probability that the back side is red too.
x-m-h3-09.thinking.0: Judge whether the events in the sample space are equally likely
x-m-h3-09.thinking.1: Compare data and theoretical calculation and revise your judgment
x-m-h3-09.thinking.2: Find the wrong line in a flawed argument
x-m-h3-09.prereq.0: Experience telling apart events with equal probability and events without equal probability
x-m-h3-09.prereq.1: Experience telling apart the number of events and the size of a probability
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose the most reasonable judgment.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write down which cases you are counting.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.hint.1: When counting cases, compare whether you count ‘cards’ or ‘sides’.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.info: The side showing on the card you drew is red.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most plausible guess now about the probability that the back is red too?
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.after: 1/2 is the guess many people think of first. A good habit is to check ‘are the two candidates really equally likely?’
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 1/2. The remaining candidates are the red-red card and the red-blue card, and the two are equally likely
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Narrowing the candidates to two cards is good. But you need to check whether the two candidates are equally likely.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 1/3. There are three cards and the red-red card is only one of them, so it is one out of three
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not reflect the fact that red is showing and went back to the first three cards.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It looks like about 1/2, but I should check whether the two candidates are equally likely
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: While stating a first guess, you also pointed out what to check.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The back is already decided, so you can't talk about a probability
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even if the back is decided, when we do not know it, we can talk about our degree of belief as a probability.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.info: I told the sides of the cards apart one by one, and there are 3 red sides in all. They are one side of the red-red card, the other side of that card, and the red side of the red-blue card. These three sides are all equally likely to be the one showing on the desk.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: How will you revise your guess with this data?
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.after: There are 3 red sides that could be the showing side, and 2 of them are sides of the red-red card. So the probability that the back is red too is 2/3.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Still 1/2. Even if there are 3 sides, there are two cards, so there are two candidates
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You counted only by the number of cards. You missed that the number of red sides differs from card to card.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 1/3. Only one of the three red sides can have a red back
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You missed that both sides of the red-red card are red. Whichever side of that card is showing, the back is red.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 2/3. Of the three red sides, two are sides of a card whose back is also red
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You counted the three red sides as equally likely cases.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Between 1/2 and 2/3, so I can't settle on one now
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.1.r.d: If you count the equally likely cases, a single value is determined.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.info: I tried it by experiment. I drew a card 600 times and put one side on the desk; red was showing 301 times, and among those the back was also red 203 times.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does this result fit the two guesses?
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.after: 203/301 ≈ 0.674 is close to 2/3 ≈ 0.667, and the difference from 1/2 is large. It also confirms that you must use only the cases that satisfy the condition (red showing) as the target.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 203/301 is about 0.67, so it is close to 2/3
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You found the ratio using only the cases where red was showing and matched it with the theoretical calculation.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 203/301 is about 0.67, but experiments have error, so I would say 1/2
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 0.67 is quite far from 0.5. Compare it with 2/3.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You used all 600 trials as the denominator. You must use only the cases where red was showing.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.o.d: An experiment has chance mixed in, so it has nothing to do with the theoretical calculation
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.st.2.r.d: An experiment does not have to be exactly the same as the theory, but it is important to compare whether they are close.
x-m-h3-09.s.s1.reflect: What assumption did your first guess of 1/2 come from, and what data made you change that assumption? How is ‘there are two candidates’ different from ‘the two candidates are equally likely’?
x-m-h3-09.s.s2.prompt: This is a solution in which a student said 1/2. Choose the first line where a problem occurs.
x-m-h3-09.s.s2.hint.0: Tell apart ‘the cards are equally likely’ and ‘red showing happens equally often’.
x-m-h3-09.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many ways each card can show a red side on the desk.
x-m-h3-09.s.s2.line.0: The showing side is red, so it is not the blue-blue card.
x-m-h3-09.s.s2.line.1: The remaining candidates are the red-red card and the red-blue card, and the two cards are equally likely.
x-m-h3-09.s.s2.line.2: So the probability that the back is red is one out of two cards, which is 1/2.
x-m-h3-09.s.s2.explain: Line 2 is the problem. Under the condition that red is showing, the red-red card has two red sides, so there are two ways for red to show, and the red-blue card has one way. So the two cards are not equally likely, and the conclusion of line 3 changes too.

x-m-h3-10.title: Are two perpendicular lines parallel?
x-m-h3-10.goal: Check, by making a counterexample with coordinates yourself, that a claim that holds in the plane may not hold in space.
x-m-h3-10.material: In a plane, ‘two lines perpendicular to one line are parallel to each other’ holds. Check with coordinates whether this also holds in space. In space, the direction vector of the line n is n = (1, 2, 2) (the components are one, two, two). Let the direction vectors of lines l and m be u = (u1, u2, u3) and v = (v1, v2, v3), and think of both as lines perpendicular to n.
x-m-h3-10.thinking.0: Reason about the difference between a plane and space
x-m-h3-10.thinking.1: Make pairs of vectors that satisfy the conditions (perpendicular, not parallel)
x-m-h3-10.thinking.2: Explain the reason for the counterexample
x-m-h3-10.prereq.0: Experience writing vectors in terms of their components in space coordinates
x-m-h3-10.prereq.1: Experience expressing the angle between two vectors and perpendicularity with vectors
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose the correct statement about the claim ‘two lines perpendicular to one line are parallel to each other’.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.hint.0: Sketch how many directions are perpendicular to a line in a plane.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how many directions are perpendicular to a line in space. (For example, directions perpendicular to a pencil standing upright)
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.a: It always holds in both a plane and space
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.a: You carried the experience in a plane straight over to space. In space, the perpendicular direction may not be only one.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.b: It holds in space but has a counterexample in a plane
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.b: Think about how many directions are perpendicular to a line in a plane.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.c: It holds in a plane and has a counterexample in space
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.c: You told apart the difference between a plane and space.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.d: It has counterexamples in both a plane and space
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.d: Check whether there is only one direction perpendicular to a line in a plane.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.explain: In a plane there is only one direction perpendicular to a line, so two perpendicular lines are parallel. In space, many perpendicular directions are possible lying in one plane, so there are cases that are not parallel.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.prompt: Choose integer components for u and v, each perpendicular to n = (1, 2, 2) and not parallel to each other, and make 2 different pairs. (A pair with u and v in swapped order is counted as the same pair.)
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write, as an equation in components, the condition for u to be perpendicular to n. Find one integer vector that satisfies that equation.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.hint.1: Find a v that is not a constant multiple of the u you found. It is easier if you set one component to 0.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.fail.c1: u is not perpendicular to n.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.fail.c2: v is not perpendicular to n.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.ok.c3: u and v are not parallel (and neither is the zero vector).
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.fail.c3: u and v are parallel, or one is the zero vector.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.explain: u = (2, −1, 0) and v = (0, 1, −1) are both perpendicular to n, and neither vector is a constant multiple of the other. The vectors perpendicular to n are many directions lying in one plane, so there are as many non-parallel pairs as you like.
